title: Linear Models
summary: Parametric models: a fixed set of coefficients fitted to the data. Linear regression has a closed-form solution; logistic and softmax regression do not and need gradient descent. Polynomial features make the same machinery fit non-linear data, and regularization keeps it from running away.

formulas.name: Linear regression prediction
formulas.note: θ₀ is the bias term; θ₁…θₙ are the feature weights; n is the number of features.

formulas.name: Vectorised prediction
formulas.note: θ is the parameter vector, x the feature vector with x₀ always equal to 1 so the dot product picks up the bias.

subtopics.title: Linear regression and the normal equation
subtopics.summary: The one model in the course with a closed-form solution: set the derivative of the MSE to zero and solve directly for the coefficients.

formulas.name: MSE cost function
formulas.note: Mean over the m training examples of the squared prediction error.

formulas.name: Normal equation
formulas.note: The value of θ minimising the MSE, computed directly. y is the vector of targets y⁽¹⁾…y⁽ᵐ⁾.

questions.prompt: Write the normal equation and say what it gives you.
questions.answer:
`θ̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹ Xᵀ y`

It gives the value of θ that **minimises the MSE cost function** — the best-fitting coefficients, computed in closed form with no iteration.

questions.prompt: The MSE cost function is (1/{{1}}) Σ (θᵀx⁽ⁱ⁾ − y⁽ⁱ⁾){{2}}, where m is the number of training examples.
In the vectorised form ŷ = θ · x, why is x₀ always set to 1?
options: So the dot product includes the bias term θ₀
questions.explanation: θ₀ × 1 = θ₀, so the intercept falls out of the same dot product as the weights. That is what `np.c_[np.ones((100,1)), X]` is doing in the code.

questions.prompt: In ŷ = h_θ(x) = θ · x, what are θ and x?
questions.answer:
**θ** is the model's *parameter vector*: the bias term θ₀ together with the feature weights θ₁ … θₙ.

**x** is the instance's *feature vector*, x₀ … xₙ, with x₀ always equal to 1.

**h_θ** is the hypothesis function using the parameters θ.

questions.prompt: A fitted model is ŷ = {{b}} + {{w}}x. What does it predict at x = {{x}}?
A model has θ₀ = {{b}}, θ₁ = {{w1}}, θ₂ = {{w2}}. Predict for the instance x₁ = {{x1}}, x₂ = {{x2}}.
Three predictions miss their targets by {{e1}}, {{e2}} and {{e3}}. Give the MSE, to 3 dp.

steps.text: MSE is the mean of the **squared** errors, so signs disappear.

questions.prompt: What does scikit-learn's LinearRegression use internally, and why?
options: SVD — more robust than matrix inversion
The normal equation with explicit matrix inversion
questions.explanation: SVD still works when #features > #examples, or when features are redundant — both cases where XᵀX is not invertible.

questions.prompt: Give the two situations where SVD works but matrix inversion does not.
questions.answer:
1. When **#features > #examples**.
2. When there are **redundant features**.

In both, `XᵀX` is singular and cannot be inverted, so the normal equation as written fails — but SVD still produces a solution.

questions.prompt: The complexity of the scikit-learn linear regression is {{1}} in the number of examples and {{2}} in the number of features.
questions.explanation: So doubling the rows doubles the work, but doubling the columns quadruples it — features are the expensive axis.

questions.prompt: Which numpy expression implements the normal equation?
questions.explanation: Reading it against θ̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy: `X_b.T.dot(X_b)` is XᵀX, inverted, then dotted with Xᵀ and y.

questions.prompt: What term describes a solution computed directly by formula rather than iteratively?
Why are linear models called parametric?
options: They have a fixed set of parameters, independent of the training set size
They only work on parametrised curves
They store the training data as parameters
questions.explanation: Contrast with kNN, which effectively keeps the whole training set — the model grows with the data.

questions.prompt: Why does the course say it is worth understanding the simpler algorithms in detail?
questions.answer: It is useful **especially when things go wrong**, or when you want to **develop your own novel algorithm**.

questions.prompt: After `lin_reg.fit(X, y)`, which attributes hold the fitted bias and weights?
Why does the MSE square the errors rather than just summing them?
questions.answer:
Because raw errors **cancel**: an overprediction of +5 and an underprediction of −5 would sum to zero and look like a perfect fit.

Squaring makes every error contribute positively, and additionally **penalises large errors disproportionately** — a single error of 10 costs more than ten errors of 1.

subtopics.title: Logistic regression
subtopics.summary: Despite the name, a classifier. It runs a linear model through the sigmoid to produce a probability, and has no closed form — so it is trained by gradient descent on the log loss.

formulas.name: Sigmoid (logistic) function
formulas.note: Maps any real number into (0, 1). σ(0) = 0.5.

formulas.name: Logistic regression prediction
formulas.note: A probability between 0 and 1, thresholded at 0.5 to give a class.

formulas.name: Log loss (per example)
formulas.expression:
c(θ) = −log(p̂)     if y = 1
c(θ) = −log(1 − p̂) if y = 0

formulas.name: Log loss (averaged)
formulas.note: The two cases combined into one expression; one term is always multiplied by zero.

questions.prompt: The course calls 'logistic regression' very bad naming. Why?
options: It is a classifier, not a regression method
It is not logistic, but exponential
It performs regression but is used for clustering
It has nothing to do with the logistic function
questions.explanation: It uses something that *looks like* linear regression inside the logistic function, but its output is a class probability.

questions.prompt: Write the sigmoid function and describe its shape.
questions.answer:
`σ(t) = 1 / (1 + e^(−t))` — equivalently `1 / (1 + exp(−t))`.

An S-shaped curve mapping all real numbers into **(0, 1)**. It passes through **0.5 at t = 0**, tends to 0 as t → −∞ and to 1 as t → +∞.

questions.prompt: A logistic model computes xᵀθ = {{t}}. Using the standard 0.5 threshold, which class does it predict — 1 or 0?

steps.text: So `p̂ > 0.5` exactly when `t > 0` — the sign of xᵀθ decides the class, no exponentials needed.
Here `t = {{t}}`, so the prediction is class **{{c}}**.

questions.explanation: Three values are worth carrying in: `σ(0) = 0.5`, `σ(t) → 1` as t → +∞, `σ(t) → 0` as t → −∞. Everything between is monotone, so a decision at the 0.5 threshold is just a question about the sign of xᵀθ.

questions.prompt: What is σ(0)?
questions.explanation: 1/(1 + e⁰) = 1/2. This is why the decision boundary sits where xᵀθ = 0.

questions.prompt: How is logistic regression trained, and why?
options: Gradient descent — there is no closed-form solution
The normal equation, as for linear regression

questions.prompt: Write the per-example logistic cost for each class, and explain its shape.
questions.answer:
`c(θ) = −log(p̂)` when `y = 1`
`c(θ) = −log(1 − p̂)` when `y = 0`

When y = 1 and p̂ is near 1, −log(p̂) is near 0 — almost no cost. As p̂ → 0 the cost goes to **infinity**: being confidently wrong is punished without limit.

questions.prompt: A single example has true label y = 1 and the model predicts p̂ = 0.2. Write down its log loss (you are not expected to evaluate the log).
questions.explanation:
The per-example log loss is `c(θ) = −log(p̂)` when `y = 1` and `−log(1 − p̂)` when `y = 0`. Only the probability assigned to the **true** label enters.

The shape is what matters: the loss is **0 when p̂ = 1** and grows without bound as p̂ → 0, so a confident wrong answer is punished far harder than a hedged one.

questions.prompt: A single example has true label y = 0 and the model predicts p̂ = 0.9. Which expression is its log loss?
questions.explanation: For `y = 0` the loss is `−log(1 − p̂) = −log(0.1)`. The model put 90% on the wrong class, so this is a large loss — which is the point of the check: substitute into the wrong branch and you get `−log(0.9)`, a small loss, and conclude the model did well.

questions.prompt: Write the averaged log loss over m examples, and explain why the two-case definition collapses into it.
questions.answer:
`J(θ) = −(1/m) Σᵢ [ y⁽ⁱ⁾ log(p̂⁽ⁱ⁾) + (1 − y⁽ⁱ⁾) log(1 − p̂⁽ⁱ⁾) ]`

Because y is 0 or 1, exactly **one term survives** per example: with y = 1 the second term is multiplied by 0, and with y = 0 the first is. It is the two-case definition written without an `if`.

questions.prompt: In the Iris example using petal width to detect Iris-Virginica, roughly where does the decision boundary fall?
questions.explanation: Where the two probability curves cross at 0.5. `log_reg.predict([[1.7], [1.5]])` returns `[1, 0]`, straddling it.

questions.prompt: In sklearn's LogisticRegression, what does a **high** value of C mean?
options: Little regularization — C is the cost of prediction errors
questions.explanation: The direction is the trap: C is the *inverse* of regularization strength, unlike alpha in Ridge and Lasso where higher means more.

questions.prompt: Contrast the direction of C in LogisticRegression with alpha in Ridge regression.
questions.answer:
They run in **opposite directions**.

**C** stands for the *cost of prediction errors*: a high C means errors matter more than small coefficients, so there is **little regularization**.

**alpha** is the weight on the penalty term: a high alpha means **more regularization**, pulling coefficients toward zero.

questions.prompt: Which method returns the probabilities rather than the class labels?
Logistic regression predicts class 1 when p̂ ≥ {{1}}, which corresponds to xᵀθ ≥ {{2}}.
The Iris example uses `y = (iris["target"] == 2).astype(np.int)`. What does this produce?
options: 1 if Iris-Virginica, else 0 — a binary target
questions.explanation: It collapses a three-class problem into a binary one, which is what plain logistic regression needs.

questions.prompt: Where exactly is the 'linear' part of logistic regression?
questions.answer:
**Inside** the sigmoid. The model computes the linear combination `xᵀθ` exactly as linear regression would, then passes that single number through `σ` to squash it into a probability.

So the **decision boundary is still linear** — it is the set of points where `xᵀθ = 0` — even though the output is a curved probability.

subtopics.title: Softmax regression
subtopics.summary: The generalisation of logistic regression to K classes. The sigmoid becomes softmax, and the log loss becomes cross-entropy.

formulas.name: Softmax function
formulas.note: s_k is the score for class k. The K outputs are positive and sum to 1.

formulas.name: Cross-entropy cost
formulas.note: The generalisation of log loss to K classes.

questions.prompt: Give the two names for the multi-class generalisation of logistic regression.
questions.answer: **Softmax regression** and **Multinomial Logistic Regression**.

questions.prompt: Write the softmax function and state its two defining properties.
questions.answer:
`p̂_k = exp(s_k(x)) / Σⱼ exp(s_j(x))` over K classes.

Properties: every output is **positive** (exp is always positive), and the outputs **sum to 1** (the denominator is the sum of all the numerators). So the vector is a valid probability distribution.

questions.prompt: Why do the softmax outputs necessarily sum to 1?
options: Every output is divided by the sum of all the numerators
Because exp is a monotone function
Because the scores are normalised before the exponential
They do not — they are only guaranteed to be positive

questions.prompt: A two-class softmax has scores s₁ = {{a}} and s₂ = {{b}}. Which class does it predict — 1 or 2?

steps.text: `p̂_k = exp(s_k) / Σⱼ exp(s_j)`. Every term shares the same denominator, and `exp` is increasing.
So the **largest score gets the largest probability** — argmax of the probabilities is argmax of the scores.

questions.explanation: This is the reason c4 can call `np.argmax(some_digit_scores)` on raw decision-function scores and get the predicted class without ever normalising them.

questions.prompt: A three-class softmax outputs p̂₁ = {{p1}} and p̂₂ = {{p2}}. What is p̂₃?

steps.text: Softmax divides by `Σⱼ exp(s_j)`, so the outputs are guaranteed to lie in [0, 1] and **sum to 1**.

questions.explanation: c6a makes the same point about the last Keras layer: softmax is there "to ensure all values are in [0.0, 1.0], and sum to 1.0". Predicted class is the argmax — here, whichever of the three is largest.

questions.prompt: What is the cost function used with softmax regression called?
Cross-entropy is J(Θ) = −(1/{{1}}) Σᵢ Σₖ y_k⁽ⁱ⁾ {{2}}(p̂_k⁽ⁱ⁾).
How is softmax regression invoked in the sklearn example?
questions.explanation: The same class as binary logistic regression, switched into multinomial mode.

questions.prompt: Given softmax probabilities, how is the predicted class chosen?
options: The class with the highest probability
The class with the highest raw score before exponentiation
questions.explanation: Note the second option fails whenever no class reaches 0.5, which is common with many classes.

questions.prompt: Model A assigns probability 0.9 to the true class; model B assigns it 0.3. Which incurs the larger cross-entropy loss on that example, and why?
options: B — the loss is −log(p̂) of the true class, which grows as p̂ falls
A — the loss rises with the probability assigned to the true class
They are equal — cross-entropy only counts whether the argmax is right
Neither — cross-entropy is only defined over a whole batch
questions.explanation: The cross-entropy cost `J(Θ) = −(1/m) ΣᵢΣₖ y_k log(p̂_k)` keeps only the term for the true class, because every other `y_k` is 0. So a single example contributes `−log(p̂_true)`: **0 when the model is certain and right**, and unbounded as the true class's probability approaches 0.

questions.prompt: How does softmax regression relate to logistic regression?
questions.answer:
It is the **generalisation to K classes**.

- The **sigmoid** generalises to the **softmax** function.
- The **log loss** generalises to the **cross-entropy** cost.

With K = 2 the two coincide.

questions.prompt: A softmax layer outputs [0.2, 0.5, 0.4]. What is wrong?
options: They sum to 1.1, so they cannot be softmax outputs
Nothing — softmax outputs need not sum to 1
questions.explanation: Softmax outputs sum to exactly 1 by construction. A sum of 1.1 means these came from something else — sigmoids applied independently, for instance.

questions.prompt: In the softmax formula, what does s_k(x) denote?
`softmax_reg.predict_proba([[5, 2]])` returns `[[6.38e-07, 5.75e-02, 9.43e-01]]`. What is predicted?
options: Class 0, since it is listed first
questions.explanation: argmax of the three probabilities. And they sum to ~1, as softmax outputs must.

questions.prompt: Does softmax ever change which class has the highest value, compared with the raw scores?
questions.answer:
No. `exp` is **monotonically increasing** and the denominator is the same for every class, so the ordering of the probabilities matches the ordering of the scores.

Softmax changes the *values* into a probability distribution; it does not change *which* is largest. That is why `np.argmax` on raw scores gives the same prediction.

subtopics.title: Polynomial regression
subtopics.summary: Non-linear data fitted with a linear model, by adding powers of the existing features. The model stays linear in its parameters; only the features change.

questions.prompt: How does polynomial regression fit non-linear data with a linear model?
questions.answer:
By **adding derived features** — powers of the existing ones — and then running ordinary **linear regression** on the expanded feature set.

The model is still linear *in the parameters*; it is the feature space that has changed.

questions.prompt: What does `PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False)` do to a single feature x?
questions.explanation: `include_bias=False` drops the constant 1 column, since LinearRegression adds its own intercept. The example shows −0.7528 becoming [−0.7528, 0.5666] — and 0.5666 ≈ 0.7528².

questions.prompt: In the 'too many new features' plot, the degree-300 curve:
options: Oscillates wildly, passing near individual points — badly overfitted
Fails to fit the training data at all
questions.explanation: Degree 1 underfits (a straight line), degree 2 fits well, degree 300 overfits spectacularly.

questions.prompt: The data is generated as `y = 0.5 * X**2 + X + 2 + noise`. Which polynomial degree should fit best?
questions.explanation: Matching the true generating degree. Higher degrees have the capacity to fit but start modelling the noise.

questions.prompt: Why is polynomial regression still called a linear model?
questions.answer:
Because it is **linear in the parameters**. The fitted function `ŷ = θ₀ + θ₁x + θ₂x²` is a curve in x, but the coefficients θ enter linearly — so the normal equation and everything else about linear regression still applies.

Only the *features* changed; the *model* did not.

questions.prompt: How does the course combine polynomial features with linear regression?
options: With a `Pipeline` holding poly_features then lin_reg
By calling fit twice in sequence

questions.prompt: A single feature x is expanded with `PolynomialFeatures(degree={{d}}, include_bias=False)`. How many features result?

steps.text: With one input feature, the expansion produces `x, x², …, x^d`.
`include_bias=False` means no constant column is added.

questions.explanation: With more than one input feature the count grows much faster, because cross terms like x₁x₂ appear too.

questions.prompt: A degree-2 model is ŷ = {{c}} + {{b}}x + {{a}}x². Predict at x = {{x}}.
Increasing the polynomial degree {{1}} model complexity and {{2}} the risk of overfitting.
What is degree-1 polynomial regression equivalent to?
What does the course call the extra x² column added before fitting?
A degree-10 polynomial is overfitting. Give two ways to address it without changing the degree.
questions.answer:
1. **More training data** — a larger sample constrains the extra capacity.
2. **Regularization** — Ridge or Lasso shrink the high-degree coefficients toward zero, so the extra terms are available but not freely used.

c3 shows exactly this: the same degree-10 model with `α = 0`, `1e-05` and `1`.

questions.prompt: With two input features x₁ and x₂ at degree 2, what does PolynomialFeatures add beyond the squares?
questions.explanation: Interaction terms are why the feature count explodes so quickly with several inputs.

questions.prompt: In the 'too many new features' plot the legend reads 300, 2, 1. Which line is closest to the underlying data-generating function?
questions.explanation: The data was generated from a quadratic, so degree 2 is the honest fit; 1 underfits and 300 overfits.

questions.prompt: Why does polynomial expansion make feature scaling more important?
questions.answer:
Because raising a feature to a power **magnifies scale differences**. A feature around 100 becomes 10 000 when squared and 10⁶ when cubed, while a feature around 1 stays near 1.

The resulting columns differ by orders of magnitude, which matters for both gradient descent and any regularization penalty that treats all coefficients alike.

subtopics.title: Learning curves
subtopics.summary: Training and validation error plotted against training set size. The gap between the two curves, and the height they settle at, diagnose which of over- or underfitting you have.

questions.prompt: What is plotted on a learning curve?
options: RMSE for train and validation against training set size
questions.explanation: Note the x-axis is training set *size*, not complexity — that is the complexity/error curve in c4.

questions.prompt: Describe the learning curves for a plain linear model on quadratic data, and what they mean.
questions.answer:
Training error starts near zero (a couple of points are fitted perfectly), rises quickly, then **plateaus around 1.7–1.8 RMSE**. Validation error starts very high, falls, and **settles at a similar level**.

The two curves are **close together and both high** — the signature of **underfitting**. The model cannot capture the pattern, so more data does not help.

questions.prompt: Describe the learning curves for a degree-10 polynomial, and what they mean.
questions.answer:
Training error stays **low** (around 0.8 or below). Validation error comes down but settles **noticeably higher**, around 1.1.

The **gap between the curves** is the signature of **overfitting**: the model does much better on data it has seen than on data it has not.

questions.prompt: A large persistent gap between training and validation curves indicates:
Both curves plateau at a high error, close together. What should you do?
options: Use a more complex model or better features
questions.explanation: This is underfitting. Adding data to an underfitting model changes nothing — the curves have already converged.

questions.prompt: When does adding more training data help, and when is it wasted?
questions.answer:
**Helps** when the model is **overfitting** — there is a gap between the curves, and more data pulls the validation curve down toward the training curve.

**Wasted** when the model is **underfitting** — the curves have already met at a high error, so more of the same data cannot close a gap that is not there.

questions.prompt: Why does the training curve start at essentially zero error?
questions.answer:
With only one or two training examples, the model can fit them **exactly** — a straight line through two points has zero error.

As examples are added the model can no longer pass through all of them, so training error rises and then levels off.

questions.prompt: In `plot_learning_curves`, the loop is `for m in range(1, len(X_train))` with `model.fit(X_train[:m], y_train[:m])`. What is it doing?
options: Refitting on progressively larger prefixes of the training set
Running m epochs of gradient descent

questions.prompt: The code appends `mean_squared_error(...)` but plots `np.sqrt(train_errors)`. What is on the y-axis?
questions.explanation: The square root of MSE. Plotting RMSE keeps the y-axis in the same units as the target.

questions.prompt: Why does the validation curve start very high?
questions.answer:
A model fitted to one or two examples **generalises terribly**. It has seen almost nothing, so its predictions on the held-out validation set are close to arbitrary.

As training data accumulates the model becomes meaningful and the validation error falls.

questions.prompt: State the course's summary of how to fix underfitting and overfitting.
questions.answer:
**Underfitting:** use a more complex model, or use better (and more) features.

**Overfitting:** use more data, or a less complex / more constrained model.

questions.prompt: At the right-hand end of a learning curve, training RMSE is {{tr}} and validation RMSE is {{va}}. How large is the generalization gap?

steps.text: The gap is validation error minus training error.
`= {{va - tr | 2}}` — a clear gap, so this model is overfitting.

questions.prompt: Training RMSE plateaus at 0.8 and validation RMSE at 1.1, with the gap not closing as data is added. Diagnose it and give two fixes.
questions.answer:
**Overfitting** — the persistent gap says the model does better on seen data than unseen.

Fixes: **more training data** (the gap is the kind that closes with data), or a **less complex / more constrained model** — a lower polynomial degree, or Ridge/Lasso regularization.

questions.prompt: Distinguish a learning curve from the training-vs-test-error-against-complexity curve in c4.
questions.answer:
A **learning curve** plots error against **training set size**, holding the model fixed. It tells you whether more *data* would help.

The **c4 complexity curve** plots error against **model complexity**, holding the data fixed. It tells you whether a different *model* would help.

Different x-axes, different questions.

questions.prompt: The learning curve code calls `train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2)`. What proportion is held out for validation?

subtopics.title: Bias–variance tradeoff
subtopics.summary: Generalization error decomposes into three parts. Two of them trade against each other along the complexity axis; the third cannot be reduced by any choice of model.

formulas.name: Error decomposition
formulas.expression: Generalization error = Bias + Variance + Irreducible error

keyFacts.definition: Error from **wrong assumptions**, e.g. assuming linear when the truth is quadratic. High bias ⇒ underfitting.
Sensitivity to **small changes in the data**. A complex model has high variance ⇒ overfitting.
**Noise in the data**. Cleaning the data might improve it; no choice of model can.

questions.prompt: Write the error decomposition and define each term.
questions.answer:
`Generalization error = Bias + Variance + Irreducible error`

**Bias** — wrong assumptions, e.g. fitting linear to quadratic data. High bias ⇒ underfitting.
**Variance** — sensitivity to small data changes. Complex model ⇒ high variance ⇒ overfitting.
**Irreducible error** — noise in the data. Only cleaning the data can help.

questions.prompt: High bias leads to {{1}}fitting; high variance leads to {{2}}fitting.
As model complexity increases, what happens to bias and variance?
questions.explanation: The slide states it both ways: high complexity ⇒ high variance, low bias; low complexity ⇒ low variance, high bias.

questions.prompt: What, if anything, can reduce the irreducible error?
questions.explanation: It is irreducible with respect to the *model*, not with respect to the *data*. The slide says cleaning the data might improve the result.

questions.prompt: In the bullseye diagram, which quadrant shows shots scattered widely but centred on the target?
questions.explanation: Centred = low bias; scattered = high variance. Tightly grouped but off-centre would be high bias, low variance.

questions.prompt: Shots tightly grouped but well away from the centre correspond to:
questions.explanation: Consistent (low variance) but consistently wrong (high bias) — an underfitting model.

questions.prompt: A linear model is fitted to quadratic data. Which error term is large, and why?
questions.answer:
**Bias** is large. The assumption that the relationship is linear is simply **wrong**, and no amount of data will fix a model that cannot represent a curve.

Variance is low — refitting on a different sample gives a similar line — but it is a similarly wrong line every time.

questions.prompt: The most performant model on new data is the one with:
options: The best tradeoff between bias and variance
The lowest bias regardless of variance
The lowest variance regardless of bias

questions.prompt: High bias plus low variance is {{1}}fitting. Low bias plus high variance is {{2}}fitting.
Which error component measures a model's sensitivity to small changes in the training data?
Decision trees are called 'unstable' in c2. Which error component is that, and what does it imply?
questions.answer:
**High variance** — a small change in the training data produces a very different tree, which is exactly the definition of variance.

It implies a fully grown tree tends to **overfit**, and it is why averaging many trees in an ensemble helps: averaging reduces variance without raising bias much.

questions.prompt: A model has bias contribution {{b}}, variance contribution {{v}} and irreducible error {{i}}. Give the generalization error, to 3 dp.

steps.text: The decomposition is `Generalization error = Bias + Variance + Irreducible error`.

questions.explanation: Only the first two terms respond to changing the model; the third sets the floor no model can go below.

questions.prompt: A dataset has irreducible error 0.4. What does that tell you about the best achievable generalization error?
questions.answer:
It **cannot go below 0.4**, whatever model you choose. Bias and variance are non-negative, so the decomposition puts a floor under the achievable error.

Practically: if you are near 0.4, stop tuning the model. The remaining error is noise, and the only route further down is better or cleaner data.

questions.prompt: Express the choice of k in kNN in bias–variance terms.
questions.answer:
**Small k** — low bias, high variance. The prediction follows individual points, so it makes few assumptions but shifts a lot with the sample.

**Large k** — high bias, low variance. Averaging over a wide neighbourhood is stable but smooths away real structure.

Choosing k *is* choosing a point on the bias–variance tradeoff.

questions.prompt: Which external reference does the course give for the bias–variance tradeoff?

subtopics.title: Ridge, Lasso and Elastic Net
subtopics.summary: Three penalties added to the MSE. Ridge shrinks coefficients, Lasso zeroes the unimportant ones, Elastic Net mixes the two. All require scaled data.

formulas.name: Ridge regression cost
formulas.expression: J(θ) = MSE(θ) + α · ½ · Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ θᵢ²
formulas.note: L2 penalty. α = 0 gives plain linear regression; α → ∞ gives a flat line through the mean.

formulas.name: Ridge closed form
formulas.note: The normal equation with αA added, which also makes the matrix invertible.

formulas.name: Lasso regression cost
formulas.note: L1 penalty. Tends to set coefficients of unimportant features to exactly 0.

keyFacts.definition: Ridge + Lasso combined. Two hyperparameters: **alpha** and **r**, the mixing ratio. Better for many features and highly correlated features.

questions.prompt: Write the Ridge cost function and describe what alpha does at its extremes.
questions.answer:
`J(θ) = MSE(θ) + α · ½ · Σ θᵢ²`

**α = 0** — the penalty vanishes, giving standard linear regression.
**α → ∞** — the penalty dominates, driving all coefficients to zero and leaving a **flat line through the mean**.

questions.prompt: Write the Lasso cost function and state its distinctive behaviour.
questions.answer:
`J(θ) = MSE(θ) + α · Σ |θᵢ|`

It uses **L1**, the absolute values, as the penalty. Its distinctive behaviour is that it **sets coefficients for unimportant features to exactly 0.0** — so it performs feature selection as a side effect of fitting.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes the Ridge penalty from the Lasso penalty?
options: Ridge sums squared coefficients (L2); Lasso sums absolute values (L1)
Ridge sums absolute values; Lasso sums squares
Ridge penalises the intercept; Lasso does not
Ridge is applied before fitting; Lasso after

questions.prompt: Which regularizer drives unimportant coefficients to exactly zero?
questions.explanation: Ridge shrinks coefficients toward zero without reaching it; Lasso can land on exactly 0, which is why it doubles as feature selection.

questions.prompt: The Ridge slide says you MUST do what before regularizing?
questions.explanation: The penalty treats all coefficients alike, so a feature on a large scale gets an artificially small coefficient and is under-penalised.

questions.prompt: Why must data be scaled before applying a regularization penalty?
questions.answer:
The penalty is applied **uniformly to every coefficient**. A feature measured on a large scale needs only a small coefficient to have the same effect, so it is penalised **less** than an equally important feature on a small scale.

The result is that the penalty's strength depends on your choice of units, which is arbitrary. Scaling first removes that.

questions.prompt: The course flags `SGDRegressor(penalty="l2")` with a warning. What is it?
options: It is a lower-case L and a 2, not the number 12
It only works with the Cholesky solver
It is deprecated in favour of alpha=
questions.explanation: In many fonts `l2` and `12` are near identical, and the resulting error is confusing.

questions.prompt: Ridge via SGD is `SGDRegressor(penalty="{{1}}")`; Lasso via SGD is `SGDRegressor(penalty="{{2}}")`.
What is Elastic Net, why use it, and what are its hyperparameters?
questions.answer:
**Ridge + Lasso** combined — both penalties at once.

**Why:** better for **many features**, and for **highly correlated features**.

**Hyperparameters:** `alpha` (overall penalty strength) and `r`, the **mixing ratio** between the two penalties.

questions.prompt: A Ridge model with α = {{a}} has coefficients {{t1}}, {{t2}} and {{t3}}. Give the value of the penalty term α·½·Σθᵢ², to 3 dp.

steps.text: The Ridge penalty is `α · ½ · Σ θᵢ²`.

questions.explanation: Squaring means signs do not matter, and large coefficients are punished disproportionately.

questions.prompt: A Lasso model with α = {{a}} has coefficients {{t1}}, {{t2}} and {{t3}}. Give the value of the penalty term α·Σ|θᵢ|, to 3 dp.

steps.text: The Lasso penalty is `α · Σ |θᵢ|` — absolute values, not squares.

questions.explanation: Note the absence of the ½ that Ridge carries — a common slip when writing the two from memory.

questions.prompt: In the Ridge example plots, increasing α from 0 to 100 on the linear data:
options: Flattens the fitted line toward a horizontal line at the mean
Makes the line pass through more data points
questions.explanation: α = 0, 10, 100 in the left plot: as α rises the slope is pulled toward zero, exactly as the α → ∞ limit predicts.

questions.prompt: Which solver does the course show for the closed-form Ridge?
Besides regularizing, what practical problem does adding αA to XᵀX solve?
questions.answer:
It makes the matrix **invertible**. Plain `(XᵀX)⁻¹` fails when features are redundant or when there are more features than examples, because XᵀX is singular.

Adding αA (for any α > 0) shifts it away from singularity, so the closed form always has a solution.

questions.prompt: In the Lasso example, the degree-10 plot uses α = 0, 1e-07 and 1. What does α = 1 produce?
options: An almost flat line — the penalty has crushed the high-degree coefficients
The wiggliest of the three curves
A model that fails to converge
questions.explanation: α = 1 is heavy regularization for this data; α = 1e-07 is nearly none, so it wiggles like the unregularized fit.

questions.prompt: You have many features, several of them highly correlated. Which regularizer does the course recommend, and why?
questions.answer:
**Elastic Net** — the slide gives exactly this case as its motivation: 'better for many features, and highly correlated features'.

It combines Ridge's stable handling of correlated features with Lasso's ability to zero out the useless ones, with `r` controlling the balance.
